summary: This proposed standard defines how to encapsulate SNMP packets in IPX, the transport used on Novell NetWare networks, so network management can work there.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP is how network managers ask devices questions. This paper shows how to send the same questions over IPX, the networking system used by Novell NetWare.

questions: how to run snmp on netware
how does snmp run over ipx
what socket does snmp use on ipx
what is the maximum snmp message size over ipx
subtitle: How to carry SNMP network management messages over Novell NetWare's IPX transport.

tldr.problem: SNMP was widely used on TCP/IP networks, but Novell NetWare environments use IPX, where UDP transport may not be available.
tldr.mechanism: SNMP packets are carried directly in IPX datagrams with Packet Type 4, and two fixed sockets are assigned: 36879 for requests and 36880 for traps.
tldr.outcome: It gives IPX-only networks a way to be managed with SNMP, while the preferred mapping for SNMP remains UDP. It obsoletes RFC 1298.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1420 as a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1298. No RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Map SNMP onto IPX
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is an integral part of the network management framework for TCP/IP-based internets. Its success led to use in networks that do not run TCP/IP. This RFC maps SNMP onto the Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX) protocol used in Novell NetWare environments.

The preferred mapping for SNMP is onto UDP, so this specification is for environments where UDP is not available. It does not suggest that an agent in a mixed environment support more than one mapping, but management stations are strongly encouraged to support mappings onto all popular transports.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the questions travel in one kind of envelope. This note is for places that only have another kind of envelope.

sections.title: Packet Type and Sockets
sections.content:
Mapping is straightforward because IPX provides a datagram service very similar to IP/UDP. SNMP packets always set the Packet Type field in the IPX header to 4 (Packet Exchange Packet).

SNMP entities receive GetRequest-PDU, GetNextRequest-PDU and SetRequest-PDU messages on socket 36879 (hexadecimal 900F), and Trap-PDU messages on socket 36880 (hexadecimal 9010). A GetResponse-PDU goes back to the IPX address and socket the request came from.
sections.plainLanguage: Questions go to one numbered mailbox and alarm messages go to another. Answers go back to whoever asked.

sections.title: Traps and Message Size
sections.content:
When a trap is sent over IPX, the agent-addr field in the Trap-PDU holds the IP address 0.0.0.0, and a manager can learn the source of the trap from the transport service.

SNMP does not require implementations to accept messages longer than 484 bytes, but this RFC recommends supporting a maximum SNMP message size of 546 bytes, the maximum allowed under IPX and the limit guaranteed to cross IPX routers that do not fragment. Implementors may use longer packets if the maximum is known.
sections.plainLanguage: Alarm messages do not have an IP address to put in the sender box, so a placeholder goes there. Messages should fit in a packet of about 546 bytes so routers do not break them.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Readers who need protection should not assume this document provides any.
sections.plainLanguage: The note does not say anything about keeping messages safe.
